qs.q: What is the primary reason why laboratory diagnosis of Hepatitis A virus infection relies on serology rather than viral isolation?
o: The virus is very difficult to culture in cell lines
The virus only replicates in the central nervous system
Viral shedding ceases years before symptom onset
Antibodies neutralize the virus rendering it non-viable
qs.e: Hepatitis A virus is very difficult to culture in standard cell lines. Diagnosis is typically made by detecting IgM anti-HAV antibodies using ELISA.

qs.q: A clinician reviews laboratory results for a patient with suspected acute viral hepatitis. A positive test for which antibody isotype is most indicative of a recent or acute infection rather than past immunity?
o: Immunoglobulin M isotype
Immunoglobulin G isotype
Immunoglobulin A isotype
Immunoglobulin E isotype
qs.e: IgM antibodies indicate an acute or recent primary infection, whereas IgG typically indicates past infection or established long-term immunity. ELISA tests routinely differentiate between these antibody classes to establish disease timing.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A serological marker used specifically to diagnose an acute Hepatitis A infection is:
o: Presence of IgM anti-HAV antibodies
Presence of IgG anti-HAV antibodies
Presence of HBsAg surface antigen
Presence of anti-HBs total antibody
qs.e: IgM anti-HAV is diagnostic of an acute Hepatitis A infection and falls to low levels within 3 months. IgG anti-HAV indicates previous infection or immunity.

qs.q: What is the primary mode of transmission for Hepatitis A virus?
o: Fecal-oral route through person-to-person contact or contaminated food and water
Parenteral exposure via infected blood plasma products and intravenous needles
Vertical transmission from infected mother to infant during delivery
Inhalation of respiratory droplets in overcrowded living spaces
qs.e: Hepatitis A is transmitted primarily via the fecal-oral route (95%), such as person-to-person contact or contaminated food and water. HAV and HEV share this fEcal transmission route.

qs.q: Which regions in Saudi children showed the highest prevalence rates of Hepatitis A due to lower socioeconomic status?
o: Border areas like Jazan and Tabook
Central urban districts like Riyadh
Eastern coastal provinces near Jubail
Western metropolitan ports like Jeddah
qs.e: The highest prevalence rate of HAV was noted at the borders in areas like Jazan and Tabook due to low socioeconomic status. Overall population numbers dropped over time with improved socioeconomic conditions.

qs.q: Which feature is characteristic of Hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection?
o: It frequently causes chronic progressive scarring
It is responsible for acute hepatitis only
Perinatal transmission is the primary route
Fulminant hepatic failure occurs in over 10%
qs.e: Hepatitis A is responsible for acute hepatitis only and does not cause a chronic disease state. Fulminant hepatic failure due to HAV is rare, occurring in less than 1% of cases.

qs.q: How is Hepatitis A virus predominantly transmitted between individuals?
o: Fecal-oral transmission route
Vertical perinatal transmission
Aerosolized respiratory droplets
Blood product transfusion route
qs.e: Transmission of HAV is almost always by person-to-person contact through the fecal-oral route. Perinatal transmission occurs rarely.

qs.q: For how long can fecal excretion of Hepatitis A virus be observed in infected infants?
o: It stops immediately before symptom onset
It resolves within 2 days of jaundice
The duration of fecal viral excretion
It ends concurrently with neutralizing IgG
qs.e: Fecal viral excretion resolves by 2 weeks after the onset of jaundice in older subjects, but the duration of fecal viral excretion is prolonged in infants. Patients remain contagious until viral shedding ceases.

ai.summary: Hepatitis A is an acute, self‑limiting viral infection transmitted fecal‑oral, presenting with jaundice and malaise. Diagnosis hinges on anti‑HAV IgM; management is supportive, with vaccination for prevention.

sections.p: Hepatitis A is caused by a non‑enveloped, single‑stranded RNA virus of the Picornaviridae family. It is acute, never becomes chronic, and is diagnosed by detecting anti‑HAV IgM antibodies in serum.

t.b: Positive indicates acute infection; negative suggests past exposure or vaccination.

Markedly raised, peak 10–20× ULN in acute phase.
Usually normal; low levels may hint at severe hepatic dysfunction.

sections.p: Acute hepatitis A is classified by clinical severity: mild (no symptoms), moderate (jaundice, fatigue), severe (fulminant hepatic failure). Fulminant cases are rare but life‑threatening.
Primary route is fecal‑oral transmission via contaminated food or water. Other risk factors include poor sanitation, travel to endemic areas, and close contact with infected individuals.
Patients develop a prodrome of fatigue, nausea, and abdominal discomfort, followed by jaundice. Hepatomegaly and mild right upper quadrant tenderness may be present.
Baseline labs include liver function tests, coagulation profile, and serology for hepatitis A, B, and C. Imaging is reserved for atypical presentations.

t.b: Elevated INR indicates impaired synthetic function; monitor for bleeding risk.
Low levels may predict severe disease.

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but include fulminant hepatic failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and rarely, extra‑hepatic manifestations such as hemolytic anemia.
Supportive care is the mainstay: adequate hydration, nutrition, and monitoring of liver function. Antiviral therapy is not indicated. Avoid hepatotoxic drugs and alcohol.

sections.p: Patients recover fully; most develop lifelong immunity. Vaccination is recommended for travelers, MSM, and people with chronic liver disease.

sections.p: Acute viral hepatitis B or C, alcoholic hepatitis, and drug‑induced liver injury can mimic HAV but differ in serology and chronicity.
Early in infection, anti‑HAV IgM may be negative; ALT can be normal in mild cases. A normal bilirubin does not exclude HAV if the patient is early.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of fulminant hepatic failure: altered mental status, severe coagulopathy, persistent vomiting, or abdominal pain with hypotension.

faq.q: Is vaccination safe for pregnant women?
faq.a: Yes, the inactivated HAV vaccine is safe and recommended for pregnant travelers.
